input.message:
I wrote `gap-report.md` with a positioning section and six ranked gaps, and `rlab cite-check` passes (95 citations of 20 papers, OK).

All novelty checks ran on 2026-11-12: 26 `rlab search` queries (OpenAlex, arXiv and Crossref, all limited to 2024 or 2025 onwards) plus 8 WebSearches. Each gap entry lists the queries it used and its closest hits. I wrote only `gap-report.md`, as agreed; ticking Gaps in `STATUS.md` and the `rlab log` / `rlab index` entries are yours to do.

**Positioning verdict (confidence medium):** We found no review that both (a) brings together head-to-head evidence on LLMs, SAST and DL detectors, including LLM+SAST hybrids, and (b) explains specific contradictions between studies through their evaluation setup, with a check of which cross-paper numbers are comparable. How our review differs from each close review:
- **kaniewski2026systematic:** covers LLM methods only and excludes studies where an LLM post-processes SAST output (p. 8). None of its future directions calls for same-benchmark comparisons across the three families.
- **zhou2025large:** stops at March 2024, has only one repository-level study, and its only LLM-vs-SAST study is the authors' own preprint.
- **sheng2025llms:** a narrative survey that neither matches results across families nor links contradictions to setup.
- **Closest competitor (outside our corpus):** a 2026 review in Computers and Artificial Intelligence (doi:10.70267/cai.v3n5.122137). It also argues that duplicates, label noise, random or temporal splits and model versions inflate results. But it compares small code Transformers with LLMs and, from its abstract, does not synthesise SAST evidence.
- **Other near misses:**
  - a 2026 SoK on LLMs in security code review and testing (doi:10.5070/sr3.62177), which is broader;
  - a 2025 ML/DL/LLM survey in Electronics (doi:10.3390/electronics14224449);
  - a 2026 dataset-focused preprint (doi:10.13140/rg.2.2.23928.40963).

Most of these near misses I read only at abstract level, which is why confidence is medium. The risk is that reviewers point to the CAI review or kaniewski for the "evaluation pitfalls" message. The review should be framed as a critical comparative review, with the cross-family, contradiction-explaining angle as its distinct contribution; gap G1's re-analysis would make that concrete.

**Ranked gaps** (feasibility means for a beginner):

| # | Gap | Confidence | Feasibility |
|---|---|---|---|
| G1 | No shared evaluation protocol; published results are never re-scored against trivial baselines (e.g. "flag everything", which gives F1 0.667 on balanced data) or at realistic vulnerability rates | medium–high | **easy**: re-analysis of published numbers, no compute; can go straight into the review as a table |
| G2 | No comparison of LLMs, SAST and fine-tuned DL on the same real code, with duplicates removed and code dated after the models' training cutoff; this absorbs the contamination candidate | medium | moderate: free tools, open 7B models, Python or Java, about 6–10 weeks |
| G3 | When LLMs filter SAST alarms, lost true vulnerabilities are not controlled per CWE on real security alerts (xiong: 22.25% missed overall, 77–85% for crypto/hashing CWEs) | low–medium | easy–moderate: OWASP Benchmark plus about 100 labelled real alerts |
| G4 | No independent replication of IRIS or RepoAudit that separates the effect of targets, metric and labeller (contradictions C2 and C6) | medium | moderate–hard: a reduced IRIS-only replication is feasible; RepoAudit is not advised for a beginner |
| G5 | No repository-level LLM-vs-SAST evidence on real CVEs for PHP or Go; JavaScript and Python have only snippet-level or synthetic-repository evidence | low–medium | moderate |
| G6 | No cost per confirmed vulnerability (including human triage time) across all three families; *Open or Frontier?* narrows this | low–medium | moderate: cheap if measured inside G2 |

**Dropped or merged candidates:**
- **Contamination as its own gap:** narrowed into G2. CWE-Trace (arXiv 2606.20502), BenchGuard (doi:10.1007/978-3-032-33260-8_22), an LLM4Code 2025 memorisation study and an ASE 2025 industry paper now cover it for LLMs alone.
- **Independent labelling and single runs:** merged into G1 and G4.
- **Statement-level and location-aware scoring:** merged into G1.
- **Workflow/IDE integration:** not reported. Only one survey supports it, I ran no dedicated three-query check, and a pilot human study already exists (doi:10.1109/csr69374.2026.11759919).
- **Whether reasoning models reduce false positives (C4):** not a gap, since tan2026think already tests it in a controlled design. It belongs in the review's discussion.

One fix during checking: a VD-S page reference was wrong and is now corrected to `[@ding2025vulnerability, p. 2]`.

**Papers recommended for addition** (not added or analysed; the 20-paper limit means you decide):
1. arXiv 2512.10485, *From Lab to Reality* (accepted at JSS): DL vs open LLMs on recent vulnerabilities kept separate in time; the closest study to G2.
2. doi:10.3390/bdcc10090303, WordPress PHP benchmark (BDCC 2026): static vs learning-based detectors with leakage controlled. It finds label quality matters more than which family is used, which supports our RQ2 thesis.
3. doi:10.3390/computers15090623, *Open or Frontier?* (Computers 2026): cost and energy of LLMs vs a fine-tuned small detector at a realistic vulnerability rate.
4. doi:10.70267/cai.v3n5.122137, the CAI 2026 review (closest competitor; must be cited).
5. doi:10.5070/sr3.62177, the SoK on LLMs in security code review and testing (second competitor).
6. arXiv 2604.13764, *RealVuln*: preprint, SAST vs LLMs on Python; the authors evaluate their own company's product.
7. Optional:
   - arXiv 2510.02534 (*ZeroFalse*) and arXiv 2610.32876 (*Trusting the Tool*, October 2026): both preprints on LLM+SAST alarm filtering;
   - arXiv 2507.21817 (*Out of Distribution, Out of Luck*, ICSE 2026): benchmark realism.

Sources (WebSearch):
- [Gnieciak & Szandala, arXiv 2508.04448](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.04448v1)
- [VulEval / SMU INK](https://ink.library.smu.edu.sg/sis_research/11291)
- [ZeroFalse](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.02534v1)
- [arXiv 2604.27714](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2604.27714)
- [PrimeVul (NSF PAR copy)](https://par.nsf.gov//servlets/purl/10594574)
- [arXiv 2506.07503](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2506.07503)
- [arXiv 2504.13474](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2504.13474)
- [arXiv 2412.15004](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2412.15004)
- [RevisitVD, arXiv 2507.16887](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.16887v3)
- [CWE-Trace, arXiv 2606.20502](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2606.20502)
- [ASE 2025 industry showcase](https://conf.researchr.org/details/ase-2025/ase-2025-industry-showcase/10/Should-We-Evaluate-LLM-Based-Security-Analysis-Approaches-on-Open-Source-Systems-)
- [arXiv 2604.08417](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2604.08417)
- [Semgrep benchmark blog](https://semgrep.dev/blog/2026/3-5x-more-true-positives-how-we-benchmark-ai-powered-detection/)
- [RealVuln, emergentmind](https://www.emergentmind.com/papers/2604.13764)
- [Endor Labs](https://www.endorlabs.com/learn/ai-sast-benchmark-2x-more-real-vulnerabilities)
- [arXiv 2609.13816](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2609.13816)
